Skip next section Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case 09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 Germany urges UN's top court to quash Israel genocide case Germany 's top legal representative has told the UN's top court that a genocide case over weapons sales to Israel , should be thrown out. The matter was brought by Nicaragua and Germany's top lawyer, Julia Monar, said the judges at the International Court of Justice lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case , dismissing Nicaragua's allegations of Berlin "facilitating genocide" as "inaccurate and distorted." Nicaragua argues that Germany's backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention. "Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Monar, told the judges. Monar said that Nicaragua failed to properly notify the German government and gave her country less than a month to reply before launching proceedings. It's typically expected that countries attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court. Monar pointed out that Berlin scrutinizes all exports of military equipment in accordance with international law. "Germany has not, since 2024, authorized an export of weapons of war, with final destination in Israel that can be used in the Gaza conflict,” she said. The German government operates what it calls a "case by case" approval process of arms sales to Israel, with the stated goal of avoiding anything that might be used in Gaza , where at least 73,000 Palestinians were killed between the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israeli civlians and late August of this year. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/12/magy.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter bejelentette, hogy meg fogják változtatni az azonos nemű párok örökbefogadásáról szóló jogszabályt Belföld Barnóczki Brigitta Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Egyértelmű, hogy meg fogjuk változtatni ezt a rendszert, nem a miniszternek, nem egy politikusnak kell döntenie ilyen esetekben, sem emberként, sem politikusként, hanem szakembereknek, akik meg tudják azt állapítani, hogy az adott kisgyermek számára milyen körülmények között érhető el az az élet, hogy utána boldog és kiegyensúlyozott tagja legyen a társadalomnak” – jelentette ki Magyar Péter szombaton, a kormány Gyermekvédelmi jelentését bemutató sajtótájékoztatójának végén. A miniszterelnök a Partizán kérdésére válaszolva úgy fogalmazott a témáról, hogy „ahogy az angol mondja, out of question”, ezt úgy értette, hogy ez már nem téma, szerinte teljesen egyértelmű, hogy nem egy politikus dolga dönteni az ilyen típusú kérdésekben. Angolul egyébként az „out of the question” kifejezés azt jelenti, kizárt, a szófordulat „the” nélkül nem létezik, a miniszterelnök válaszából viszont egyértelműen kiderült, hogy arra gondolt, nem politikus dolga dönteni a kérdésben. A jelenleg hatályos, a Fidesz által korábban gyermekvédelminek nevezett, valójában azonban jogvédők szerint is melegellenes törvény szerint csak a házaspárokat illeti meg az örökbefogadás lehetősége Magyarországon, minden más esetben a mindenkori családpolitikáért felelős miniszter hozzájárulására van szükség az örökbefogadáshoz. Magyar Péter válasza alapján ezen változtatni fog a kormány. Az Orbán-kormány éveket töltött azzal, hogy Brüsszel, Soros György és a migránsok mintájára az LMBTQ-közösségből is ellenségképet gyúrjon. A próbálkozás nemhogy nem sikerült, a Telexnek nyilatkozó kutatók szerint a homofób retorika és a melegellenes intézkedések sora a fiatalok elvesztéséhez és a Fidesz–KDNP katasztrofális választási vereségéhez is hozzájárult, a Medián kutatása alapján pedig az emberek több mint kétharmada támogatja, hogy az azonos nemű párok összeházasodhassanak, és gyereket fogadhassanak örökbe. Az új kormánypárt egyelőre a gesztusokon túl hallgat arról, hogy meglépik-e a törvények eltörlését, vagy lépnek-e az egyenjogúság felé. A melegek örökbefogadásával és az Orbán-kormányok melegellenes politikájával ebben a videóban foglalkoztunk részletesen. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-to-tr.text: The European Commission will continue to seek an international agreement on AI security, despite U.S. resistance, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Tuesday. "The U.S. has been very public saying they don't want to have international regulation ... because they have concerns that it's hindering innovation,” Virkkunen said on the stage of the RAID Conference in Brussels in response to questions by POLITICO. U.S. President Donald Trump has brushed away concerns about AI existential risks as a "hoax," and declared his opposition to global regulations. The EU takes a different view, having offered its support for last week's initiative for an international safety body to monitor AI led by Finland and Norway, and signed by 20 other countries. Advertisement Advertisement "We have a different approach because we think that, if you are regulating in a pro-innovation manner, it's also a good basis for innovation that people have trust in those technologies," said Virkkunen, the EU Commissioner responsible for technology. She praised the EU’s landmark 2024 AI Act as a strong regulatory basis for tackling challenges posed by AI bots. Calls to slow down technological development and strengthen international governance have grown as reports of AI agents going rogue come to light. On Tuesday, OpenAI reportedly said it would not release its latest model out of safety concerns, while rival Anthropic will note AI's "risk to humanity" in its upcoming IPO documents. "This summer, we have seen AI agents act in a ways we maybe never thought possible," Virkkunen noted. "Agents escaping their environment, agents inserting malicious code and agents using deception on humans." The Finnish-born European Commissioner told the audience that discussions are already taking place in international forums such as the G7, because "people have serious security concerns, because there are no international rules about the safety and security." "The European Union will continue to promote this internationally. We should have agreements about the safety and security of AI. At the same time, we continue to enforce our rules," she said, also calling for greater cooperation in the meantime among national AI safety organizations. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/06/yeme.text: Yemeni government forces launched a major offensive to retake areas around the Bab el-Mandeb strait from the Houthis, as Pakistan and Turkey agreed to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia and the Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport, oil facilities and military bases in a widening war.Yemeni officials said forces allied with the internationally recognised government retook on Monday the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait, a vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, the officials said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under air cover by a Saudi military coalition.In turn, the Houthis' military spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree said in a pre-recorded statement that the group used ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh and an oil refinery in the Red Sea city of Rabigh.Also attacked were Abha airport, military facilities in Khamis Mushait and other "critical sites" in the cities of Najran and Jizan, he claimed.The US Embassy in Riyadh warned US citizens on social media to be vigilant about possible drone or missile attacks.The group formally known as Ansar Allah said they had captured more territory in the southwestern part of Yemen, taking a key town in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward a strategic provincial capital in the region.The Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Major General Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets supported government forces. He said the coalition secured "air protection" of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets.Yemen Dawn advancesThe escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen's war after a four-year ceasefire.On Sunday, the Houthis captured the town of Turbah, which sits on a main road linking the provincial capital of Taiz with the port city of Aden, which serves as an interim seat of Yemen's government. Over the years, the town was a major post for government forces defending Taiz.Earlier, the Houthis seized several villages and areas on Taiz's outskirts, paving the way for the group to encircle Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.The Houthis made a swift push on the country's western coast on the Red Sea in early September, capturing the strategic city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, gains that enabled them to control the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb, through which 12% of global trade transits.The Saudi-backed government said Sunday it was mobilising troops across government-held areas.Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, said in a televised speech that the operations were aiming at "recovering the remaining territories" controlled by the Houthis. He called on the international community to provide support to his government.Hours after al-Alimi's declaration, the Saudi military spokesperson al-Malki vowed "full operational support" to Yemeni government forces until the Houthis are "eliminated."Al-Alimi said in a post on X on Monday that the operation — dubbed Yemen Dawn — had started with the aim of "restoring state institutions, liberating" the Houthi-controlled capital Sana'a, and ending "the Houthi terrorist militia coup".Al-Nazili said government forces were carrying out a "strategic offensive" on the capital. The Houthi media office reported multiple airstrikes on their territories, including Sana'a.The group's taking of Turbah will likely constrain government forces' ability to reinforce and resupply front-line positions across Taiz province and the provincial capital of Taiz, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.Also on Monday, the foreign and defence ministers of Pakistan and Turkey agreed with Saudi Arabia to deploy military forces to the kingdom under their defence pact.A joint statement released by Pakistan's Foreign Ministry after an emergency meeting in Riyadh did not specify troop numbers, identify which countries would contribute forces or give a deployment timetable.The three countries condemned what they described as attempted attacks on Mecca and Medina, as well as continuing attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic facilities. The statement did not identify who was responsible.Concerns over humanitarian crisis spikeYemen's war began in 2014 when the Houthis launched an offensive from their northern stronghold, capturing Sana'a and forcing the government to flee into exile in Saudi Arabia. It created one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters, resulting in the deaths of more than 150,000 people.The latest bout of violence has killed at least 959 people and wounded over 4,200 others, according to the WHO. The flare-up forced about 174,097 people to flee their homes inside Yemen, according to the UN migration agency. More than 3,000 others fled across the waters into Djibouti, the agency reported.Last week, Yemen's health ministry — part of the internationally recognised government — warned about the war's impact on health facilities and medical staff across Taiz province.The ministry said in a statement on Friday that health facilities in coastal, western and southern areas of the province have closed or are barely functioning.A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting" and condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia.The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

China’s AI strategy tells a different story The Weight of Gold: Capitalism and the limits of rebellion A last chance for peace: Can Tehran move closer to Makkah before war erupts China-US relations: Trump and Xi’s diplomacy masks a fragile rivalry Indonesia turns to India for fuel security: A strategic shift in Asia’s energy landscape Sri Lanka faces growing cybercrime threat as more than 1,000 suspects are arrested From Dhaka 1971 to Peshawar 2026: How Pakistani Generals override democracy Home Featured Zelensky’s pressure tactics could backfire as Trump refuses to be bullied Damsana Ranadhiran Update Time : Thursday, October 15, 2026 Ukraine’s president has repeatedly pressured Western leaders through public criticism, but confronting Donald Trump could jeopardize Kyiv’s vital military and diplomatic support. Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky has developed a familiar strategy for dealing with Western leaders who disagree with him: criticize their decisions publicly, question their judgment, and suggest that their policies ultimately benefit Russian President Vladimir Putin. While this approach has sometimes helped Kyiv secure Western support, applying the same tactics to US President Donald Trump could carry serious consequences for Ukraine. The central question is whether Zelensky can continue raising the political cost of refusing Ukraine’s demands without creating an even greater cost for his own country. On October 9, Zelensky reportedly described Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel as a “weak decision by strong partners.” His criticism came as Ukrainian and American officials were discussing ways to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Zelensky argued that the move would provide Moscow with additional resources to sustain its military campaign. Kyiv has legitimate reasons to oppose measures that strengthen Russia’s economy during wartime. However, disagreement over policy does not automatically demonstrate weakness or disloyalty. Washington must also consider American economic interests, energy prices, and the possibility of negotiating an agreement. By turning policy disputes into public confrontations, Zelensky risks alienating the very partners on whom Ukraine depends. Europe has already experienced this pressure Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz repeatedly faced Zelensky’s public criticism over Berlin’s approach to Russia. In March 2022, addressing Germany’s parliament, Zelensky invoked the symbolism of Berlin’s historical divisions and urged Scholz to tear down what he described as a new wall separating Europe. His message was clear: Germany should abandon its economic ties with Russia and strengthen its support for Ukraine. By June, Zelensky was openly questioning whether Germany could balance its relationship with Russia against its commitment to Ukraine. He also criticized delays in German weapons deliveries. Berlin had legitimate reasons to reconsider its dependence on Russian energy and support Ukraine’s defense. Nevertheless, German policymakers also had to consider energy security, economic stability, military resources, and domestic political opinion. Zelensky’s rhetoric often presented these complicated decisions as a simple choice between supporting Ukraine and helping Russia. Such arguments could generate public pressure, but they also risked making diplomatic compromise politically difficult. The tension continued in November 2024, when Scholz spoke by telephone with Putin. Although the German leader demanded the withdrawal of Russian troops and reaffirmed support for Ukraine, Zelensky criticized the conversation as opening a “Pandora’s box.” The episode highlighted a fundamental diplomatic disagreement. Kyiv wanted to maintain Russia’s international isolation, while Berlin believed that communication with Moscow could still serve a purpose. Speaking to an adversary does not necessarily mean abandoning opposition to that adversary’s actions. If every diplomatic conversation with Putin is treated as betrayal, the prospects for meaningful negotiations become increasingly limited. Disputes with Poland and Slovakia Zelensky’s confrontational approach has also strained relations with other European partners. In September 2023, a dispute over Ukrainian grain imports triggered tensions with Poland. At the United Nations, Zelensky criticized some European countries for performing solidarity while indirectly helping Russia. Although he did not name Poland, Warsaw interpreted the remarks as criticism of its position and summoned Ukraine’s ambassador. Polish leaders faced pressure to support Ukraine while also protecting domestic farmers from market disruption. These competing responsibilities were not necessarily incompatible, but Zelensky’s public criticism made the disagreement more personal. Relations with Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico also deteriorated amid a dispute over Russian gas transit in January 2025. Zelensky criticized Fico personally and accused him of pursuing arrangements that benefited Moscow. Such tactics may appeal to audiences sympathetic to Ukraine, but they can also encourage foreign leaders to resist Kyiv’s demands rather than seek compromise. Wartime solidarity cannot eliminate the domestic economic and political responsibilities of Ukraine’s partners. Trump is different from European leaders Zelensky’s confrontation with Trump is particularly risky because the American president has demonstrated little patience for public pressure from foreign leaders. Before Trump returned to office in January 2025, Zelensky questioned his understanding of how to end the war and criticized his running mate, JD Vance. In February 2025, tensions escalated during a televised Oval Office meeting, where disagreements over diplomacy, American support, and Ukraine’s negotiating position erupted into a public argument. Trump rejected Zelensky’s approach and challenged the Ukrainian president’s handling of the relationship. The confrontation exposed the limitations of Kyiv’s diplomatic strategy. Zelensky has frequently appealed to Western leaders by emphasizing Ukraine’s sacrifices and warning that their decisions could benefit Putin. Trump, however, has presented himself as a leader determined to negotiate on his own terms. Publicly questioning Trump’s judgment is unlikely to be the most effective way to persuade him. More importantly, the United States remains a critical source of military assistance, intelligence cooperation, and diplomatic support for Ukraine. Kyiv cannot assume that Washington will continue providing these resources regardless of political disagreements. Following Zelensky’s criticism of the diesel decision, Trump suggested that Ukraine might need a different leader capable of reaching an agreement. That statement does not establish a formal American policy to remove Zelensky, but it signals growing frustration with Kyiv’s negotiating approach. If Washington concludes that Ukraine’s leadership is obstructing a settlement, the consequences could extend beyond diplomatic tensions to the future terms and scale of American assistance. Ukraine cannot afford to lose Washington A serious deterioration in relations between Kyiv and Washington could weaken Ukraine’s military position and complicate its efforts to negotiate favorable security arrangements. Russia could benefit from divisions among Ukraine’s supporters without winning a decisive battlefield victory. Uncertainty over weapons supplies, intelligence sharing, or American diplomatic backing could create additional challenges for Kyiv. Zelensky may believe that public criticism will encourage American lawmakers, European governments, and voters to pressure Trump into changing course. Such an approach can sometimes generate political leverage, but it depends on the other side accepting the argument that refusing Kyiv is more costly than accommodating it. Trump may instead interpret repeated criticism as evidence that Zelensky is unwilling to compromise. That would be a dangerous miscalculation for Ukraine. Nevertheless, the responsibility for achieving peace does not rest solely with Kyiv. Russia launched its full-scale invasion, and any sustainable settlement must address Ukraine’s security concerns and the danger of renewed aggression. Washington must also recognize that pressuring Ukraine into an agreement without credible safeguards could produce only a temporary pause in the conflict. The challenge is to pursue negotiations without undermining Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. Public pressure is not the same as diplomatic strength Zelensky has used moral appeals and public criticism to keep Ukraine at the center of international attention. His strategy has helped mobilize sympathy and support, but its effectiveness has limits. Western governments have their own security interests, economic pressures, and electoral responsibilities. They may support Ukraine while disagreeing with particular policies or questioning whether continued fighting can produce a better outcome than negotiations. Treating every disagreement as assistance to Putin risks alienating partners and narrowing the space for compromise. A more effective strategy would allow Kyiv to defend its interests firmly while recognizing that private negotiations can achieve more than public humiliation. Zelensky does not need to abandon Ukraine’s security demands, but he must understand that maintaining Western support requires cooperation as well as pressure. Trump, meanwhile, must balance his desire for a negotiated settlement against the strategic consequences of weakening Ukraine’s position too severely. Ultimately, Zelensky faces a choice: continue escalating his public confrontation with Washington or adopt a more measured approach that protects Ukraine’s vital relationship with the United States. The tactic that once pressured European leaders may not work against Trump. Worse, it could persuade the American administration that Kyiv itself has become an obstacle to an agreement. For a country heavily dependent on Western support, that is a risk Zelensky can ill afford to take. https://www.novinite.com/view_news.php?i.text: iNews Novinite Econ DoctorOnline Jenite Div Sporta FitWell Sportuvai Peika Programata News in English BUSINESS POLITICS WORLD SOCIETY SPORTS Latest Culture Crime · Hotels 5* · Hotels 4* · Hotels 3* · Apartment Houses · Bar&Restaurants · Rent-a-car · Casino · Sport · Mountain resorts · Sea resorts · Education · Entertainment · Shopping · Health Clinics · Beauty Zone · Public Safety · Business Finance Best in BG Novinite Insider · Radisson Blu · 4 Seasons · French Survey · Investors Survey · Austrian Survey · Italian Survey · US Survey · Greek Survey · Dutch Survey Special Topics Editorial Interview Features Opinions Expert Voices Diplomatic Channel A Tired Debate, a Clear Divide: Why Sunday’s Runoff Is About Bulgaria’s Place in Europe Tweet Share Send to Kindle In Thursday night’s debate on the Bulgarian National Television, the only one before Sunday’s runoff, Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov were asked about the war next door. “Peace can only be achieved through negotiations,” Yotova said. “Russia cannot be excluded from this process.” For the Black Sea, where drones have hit five merchant ships in Bulgaria ’s economic zone this month, she proposed a meeting of the six littoral states, Russia among them, to agree a moratorium on hostilities. Gyurov ’s reply was shorter. “A moratorium, expressed merely as a wish, does not constitute a defense strategy. Silence is not defense.” He asked her to call the aggressor state by its name and then: “Did you call Putin to ask him to stop the war?” That exchange captured what Sunday’s runoff has become. Presidential elections in Bulgaria are usually fought over domestic grievances, above all corruption and the cost of living. This one started that way. By its final week, Rumen Radev’s government had told voters the runoff was a choice “between peace and war,” refused to name Russia over the Black Sea strikes and hinted that Romania had invited further attacks by doing so. On Thursday, the two candidates gave opposite answers to the question Radev had posed. What the Debate Showed It was not a memorable night for either candidate. Both looked tired, with Yotova on the attack for most of the two hours and Gyurov on the defensive, replying with reasoned but brief and low-energy answers, as if Gyurov were the incumbent and Yotova the ambitious opposition figure. Neither landed a knockout blow. The substance, though, was unusually clear. Yotova filled out her position with history and diplomacy. She argued that sending more weapons to Ukraine only adds to the casualties, that the war began in 2013 and 2014 and not in 2022, and that Russia cannot be brought to the table through ultimatums. Gyurov said the Black Sea “has become more insecure than the Persian Gulf,” the result of “a policy of appeasement,” and that an aggressor stops only “when the cost of an attack becomes prohibitively high.” On Bulgaria ’s place in Europe he put it more bluntly still: “If you aren’t at the table, you’re on the menu.” The debate also exposed where each candidate stands toward the government. Asked by moderator Poli Zlatareva whether she would uphold the policies of the government and Progressive Bulgaria from the presidency, Yotova would not answer, suggesting the question was a talking point of “the people who nominated Gyurov.” Gyurov said he was “an independent candidate” with “no connection” to the parties supporting him. The claim is generous to himself, since he chaired We Continue the Change’s parliamentary group and runs with the backing of PP, DB and the DSB. But he answered the question, and she did not, and it matters because of what an aligned presidency would be aligned with. Her other answers suggested what that alignment would look like. She said she would sign the government's next budget "even if, through some very unfortunate turn of events, you were to win," which is accurate, since her current term runs until January 2027. She called for scrapping the restricted list of caretaker prime ministers, echoing a proposal Radev's government announced in August. Asked about a deputy prime minister who divides the press into "good" and "bad" media while the government's press office campaigns for her, she replied that freedom of the media means freedom of opinion "for the Deputy Prime Minister, for the Prime Minister, and for everyone else." Several of her claims do not survive a check. She said the deal with Turkey's Botas came about because "Kiril Petkov and Asen Vassilev cut off Russian gas supplies to Bulgaria overnight." In fact Gazprom halted deliveries in April 2022 after Sofia refused to pay in rubles, and the Botas agreement was signed in January 2023 by the caretaker government of Galab Donev, whom Radev appointed. Bulgaria has since come to owe Botas hundreds of millions of dollars. She presented Gyurov 's security agreement with Ukraine as a commitment to send Bulgarian soldiers as peacekeepers, but Radev himself told parliament that the agreement contains no commitment to specific actions and his government has not terminated it. And when Gyurov argued that Bulgaria should shape EU decisions instead of waiting to veto them, Yotova said she could not recall a single Bulgarian veto, although Sofia blocked the start of North Macedonia's EU accession talks from late 2020, with Radev's backing, the very dispute the two argued over minutes later. Gyurov was not immune either. His suggestion that the arrests of DPS mayors were the result of a broken deal between Progressive Bulgaria and DPS is speculation for which he offered no evidence. Yotova , in turn, accused him of describing the arrests as a new "Revival Process," the communist-era campaign against Bulgarian Turks, which he denied ever saying, and she cited no source. Former prime minister Kiril Petkov, whose government Yotova attacked over the French proposal on North Macedonia, responded after the debate that it was his cabinet that turned the veto into the French proposal backed by the whole EU, that his trip to Skopje with Yotova had been for the opening of a friendship club, unrelated to the negotiations, and that it was Russia that cut off gas supplies. Petkov is a partisan voice, but on Gazprom the record bears him out. If the government wants this vote to be about where Bulgaria stands in the world, voters are entitled to take the question seriously. The answer the evidence points to is that Bulgaria 's security lies with its allies in the European Union and NATO and that the presidency should be held by someone willing to say so clearly. How the Governing Camp Reframed the Vote The shift began the morning after the first round, when Yotova 's 20-point poll lead had shrunk to 2.8 points in the actual count. Speaking at the Sofia Economic Forum on October 26, Radev framed the runoff as a choice between peace and war and urged voters to "send the 'assembly' to oblivion," his term for the coalition of GERB, DPS and PP-DB that preceded his government. He accused Andrey Gyurov of entering the race to protect Delyan Peevski and the official page of Progressive Bulgaria has since claimed that Gyurov met Peevski, which Gyurov calls a lie and for which no evidence has been offered. The message went out through the Council of Ministers' official channels. When Gyurov 's team complained to the Central Election Commission , the government's press office responded by instructing media to report the prime minister's words accurately, prompting the Association of European Journalists in Bulgaria to warn of conditions for censorship. A government that uses the state's machinery to tell voters that one candidate means war has no grounds to complain when the vote is read as a referendum on its foreign policy. The online campaign has followed the same pattern. A Sensika Technologies report on the campaign's social media found coordinated, artificially amplified activity on both sides: a network of Facebook groups with about 320,000 members, built around Nikolay Barekov and the BNews site, was renamed to back Yotova at the end of August, while anonymous TikTok "resistance" accounts posted 544 videos praising Gyurov. In neither case did the researchers find a direct link to the official campaigns. The report also found the Russian network Rybar presenting Radev and Yotova as a "stability factor" and identical texts circulating between Revival-linked Telegram groups and channels tied to Russian networks, though it cautions that timing alone does not prove coordination. Who Has Lined Up Behind Whom The endorsements of the past four days tell their own story. Behind Yotova stand Progressive Bulgaria , the Bulgarian Socialist Party and Georgi Parvanov's ABV. On October 28 Ivelin Mihaylov of Greatness, who finished fifth with 57,643 votes, called on his supporters to vote for her, describing it as a step toward "a change in governance" and insisting it was no choice of the lesser evil. Revival's Kostadin Kostadinov has stopped short of a formal endorsement, but he ruled out Gyurov entirely, promising that "Andrey Gyurov will not receive a single vote from Revival" and predicting that his voters would split between Yotova , abstention and the "I do not support anyone" box. In the same briefing he complained that the European Council had blamed Russia for the Black Sea attacks without evidence, and after the latest strike he suggested the targeted ship had "probably carried weapons," again without evidence. He told BGNES that Revival voters might have acted differently had Yotova formally asked for their support, and in the same remarks announced that he would travel to Moscow for a BRICS-related meeting where he is due to meet Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chair of Russia's Security Council, once again. The Party of European Socialists has endorsed Yotova , which led Ivaylo Mirchev of Yes, Bulgaria to ask how she squares that with tacit backing from a party that sits alongside Germany's AfD in the European Parliament. Gyurov has the support of We Continue the Change, Democratic Bulgaria and the DSB, and a deputy chair of the Union of Democratic Forces has called for a vote for him. MECH's Radostin Vassilev has not formally endorsed Gyurov either, though on election night he told his voters that they should vote "under no circumstances for Iliana Yotova ," adding: "In other words, they either vote for Andrey Gyurov or stay home." GERB and DPS have said nothing. Political analyst Berkay Chokdzhan argued on Bulgarian National Radio that both kept their voters at home in the first round to measure their electoral weight, and he doubts the arrests of DPS mayors were the main reason for the boycott. A candidate is not responsible for everyone who votes for them. Still, a camp that now gathers the parties most reluctant to name Russia as the aggressor in the Black Sea has defined itself, whether Yotova intended it or not. The Black Sea Paradox Nothing captures the governing camp's position better than Radev's remark about Romania. At the same forum on October 26 he said that Romania had pointed to Russia as the force behind the drone strikes and that new attacks on ships in Romanian waters had followed. Damyana Veleva of Svobodna Tochka summed up the logic with a schoolyard image: you point at the bully, and your neighbor scolds you for causing the next fight because you did not keep quiet. In Romania, the reaction ranged from former interim prime minister Cătălin Predoiu's call for "consistency, logic and mutual solidarity" to commentator Cosmin Prelipceanu's verdict on Digi24 that the remark was "pure delirium." The paradox is plain. Romania, where ships were sunk and sailors died off Constanța, is cast as partly responsible for naming the aggressor, while the aggressor goes unnamed. If accusing Russia provokes Russia, then Sofia already knows who is behind the attacks and has chosen not to say so. Radev has instead cited Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who, by his account, assured him she had no information that the drones were Russian. The policy has not even bought Bulgaria the quiet it implies. On October 28 the container ship Contship Jet, bound for Constanța, was hit by three sea drones about 17 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra, the fifth attack in Bulgaria 's own economic zone this month. A French patrol aircraft spotted it. Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov said the drones could not be intercepted because the attack took place outside Bulgarian territorial waters. Romania, meanwhile, has used F-16s to shoot down drones over its territory and summoned Russia's ambassador, and its new foreign minister, Dan Neculaescu, called the strikes a deliberate escalation in violation of international law. Sofia has asked allies for patrol aircraft, and that help is welcome, but it still will not name the threat that Bucharest has named. The pattern extends onshore. On October 9, eight of the 18 antennas at a Starlink ground station near Sofia that supports Ukraine's defense were set on fire . Two 19-year-old German citizens were arrested in Duisburg on October 23, and Lithuanian prosecutors, who have charged them over a similar attempt in Vilnius, are examining possible links to Russia. Ivaylo Mirchev of Yes, Bulgaria says a partner intelligence service warned Sofia at least a week in advance, a claim the government has not confirmed. Radev chose to brief journalists instead of answering in parliament. The Case for Yotova and Its Limits Yotova 's supporters have a case, and it deserves a fair hearing. Bulgaria is a small country next to a war and caution has real value. Insisting on evidence before blaming a nuclear power is defensible diplomacy, and a president who promises that no Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine speaks to a fear that many voters genuinely hold. After five years of political chaos, there is also something to be said for a head of state who works with the government instead of against it. The trouble is that caution has become an excuse for passivity. The pledge on soldiers addresses a decision that belongs to parliament, which already ruled out participation in the fighting in February 2025, so it protects voters from a danger nobody proposed. The demand for proof has hardened into a refusal to draw the conclusion that Bulgaria 's own allies, including the European Council and the government in Bucharest, have already drawn. And the language of peace has done nothing to stop ships burning off Kaliakra. Bulgaria 's security in the Black Sea depends on Romanian coordination, French aircraft and NATO assets, and every hint that the victims brought the attacks on themselves makes that help harder to keep. Gyurov 's Answer Gyurov 's reply came in a video address this week. "While those in power frighten us with war, it is precisely their inaction that allows the war to reach our shores," he said. "The government cannot, does not know how to and fails to protect its citizens." He accused Radev and Yotova of acting as observers who "do not inform the population, hide and refuse to take clear action," and dismissed Progressive Bulgaria 's claim about a meeting with Peevski as "desperate lies." Not every line was measured. Comparing the government's use of the word "warmongers" to the vocabulary of Goebbels and Stalin is the kind of escalation his campaign should leave to others. The substance, though, has been consistent. After the October 13 strikes he called for consultations under Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which means talks among allies and no military commitment. He has argued for working with Romania and Turkey and for using EU and NATO mechanisms to protect shipping, and on Ukraine he speaks of support for a lasting peace backed by security guarantees. A fabricated quote claiming he would send Bulgarian troops to Ukraine was debunked by Factcheck.bg . His central promise is modest and that is its strength.
